newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China trade in people puts a price on human life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China trade in people puts a price on human life.

text.p: Few parents in any nation could ever express just how much they value their children, but thousands of families in China know exactly how much theirs are worth -- because they paid cash for them.
Nearly two decades of economic reform have revived an ancient trade in human life fuelled in part by the traditional desire for a son to carry on the family name.
Police in the northern Chinese city of Handan were recently recognised for rescuing 51 abducted children and arresting 61 members of a gang that had been selling them.
Kidnappers pluck young children, usually boys, from the streets of cities and towns and spirit them far away into China's rural vastness for sale to barren couples.
"From kidnapped and sold people who have been rescued, we know that most of the kidnapped children go to childless families," said an official of the All-China Women's Association.
Young boys are not the only commodity to be found on China's underground people market. Girls and young women are on sale as wives for single farmers or fodder for the nation's booming sex industry.
HUMAN TRAFFICKING REVIVED BY REFORMS
Authorities caught more than 130,000 people-traffickers between 1991 and 1996, and rescued more than 70,000 women and children who had been sold, state media has reported.

Police and government officials are reluctant to give more detailed figures or to discuss their efforts to curb the trade, a legacy of China's pre-communist past that has roared back to life as economic reform loosens once-strict social controls.
"Cases of the kidnapping and sale of women and children often occur," said a member of the specialist bureau set up by China's police to crack down on the trade.
"Attacking this kind of criminal activity and protecting the legal interests of women and children is something public security organisations do every day," said the police official.
Analysts and newspaper reports put the price of a stolen son or daughter at anything from 2,000 to 5,000 yuan ($240-$600).
The cost in human suffering is incalculable.
Anguished parents roam the country in search of their loved ones, often travelling thousands of kilometres and driving themselves into destitution and despair.

"The kidnapping and sale of women and children does not just bury countless women and children in the deepest misery, it also creates huge suffering for countless families," wrote the father of one abducted woman in a plea to the state for action.
"Families are destroyed and lives are lost," he wrote in a letter quoted late last month by the China Women's News in a front-page report on the modern-day slave trade.
AUTHORITIES TARGET BUYERS

Official efforts to find and punish kidnappers had cut the number of kidnapping cases but had failed to eliminate the underground trade, prompting police to turn their focus toward the source of demand, the official newspaper said.
"The heaviest blows will be aimed at the buyers' side of the market," the newspaper quoted a recent national police conference as concluding.
The eastern province of Shandong had cut the number of kidnap and human-sale cases to 293 in 1994 from 3,290 in 1991, partly by making sure buyers were punished, it said.
Such tactics, along with improved propaganda and social mobilisation, would help to stamp out the illegal trade nationwide, it said.
But foreign experts and Chinese analysts said it won't be easy to end a trade born of desperation.

Most buyers are from poor and backward areas who have few alternative means of acquiring that longed-for male heir. Childless couples who buy a son often lavish love and affection on him and some children refuse to return to their real parents even after being found.

Moreover, the traditional preference for sons and modern labour migration patterns have left many villages bereft of marriageable women, leaving poor farmers with no choice but to buy a bride since they lack the resources to attract a mate in any other way.
SOCIAL ATTITUDES COMPLICATE ENFORCEMENT

Local authorities are often sympathetic and do little to punish those known to have bought a family member, while whole village communities sometimes unite to fend off outside law enforcers, social analysts say.

Some victims eventually come to terms with their new situation despite the abuse and rape of some stolen women, since marriage and the birth of a child can make it socially impossible ever to return home.
Even greater social hazards are faced by young women -- many snared by traffickers who prey on informal city job markets for rural migrants -- who are forced into prostitution.
The limited figures published by state media show that the number of cases of kidnapping and sale far outnumber the victims rescued, suggesting that many never go back.

Some analysts suggest that the trade in human lives will only grow. China's strict family planning policy is seen as further raising the ratio of men to women, as rural families abort or kill female offspring to make sure their legally allotted one child is a son.
But one Western expert familiar with China's efforts to end the trade echoed official optimism that the tide may already have turned.
"From the information we have, it is an issue that had peaked a few years ago... and there has been some reduction over the last couple of years," said the expert, who declined to be identified.

China was growing more willing to publicly acknowledge the issue and to allow cooperation with the international community, although the sheer size of the country would always make it difficult to completely eliminate the trade, he said.
"In China it's not easy to control things... This is a gigantic country," he said.
